AlternateTargets: a named state of complete command
Senses.Explanation: The three graphs form an established phonetic borrowing, rendered here as 'complete command'; the Chan corpus determines its usable content through named compounds and direct definitions. The term occurs 4,852 times in 382 allowed texts. Huineng defines 'complete command of the single conduct' as 'at every place, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always carry one straight mind' (一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也). The same address rejects the claim that 'not raising thought while constantly sitting unmoving is complete command of the single conduct' (常坐不動，妄不起心，即是一行三昧), saying that this understanding is like the insentient and blocks the Way. Mazu's record says that thought after thought becoming still is called 'complete command of the ocean seal,' which 'takes in all things as a hundred thousand different streams return together to the great sea' (喚作海印三昧攝一切法如百千異流同歸大海). It also says beings remain within 'complete command of the nature of the teaching' while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the six sense-roots, and carrying out every action (法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為). Xuansha says that buddhas are people's 'self-receiving complete command' and that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it; when asked what that complete command is, he replies, 'What use are so many modes of complete command?' (用如許多三昧作麼). The word therefore appears as the head of explicitly named states or domains whose predicates vary by text; this entry does not collapse those names into one imported definition.
Senses.Note: Direct formula harvesting found many definitions of compounds rather than one definition of the bare headword. The article foregrounds the richest Chan self-definitions and Xuansha's corrective answer. The Chinese is historically a phonetic borrowing, but this English dictionary translates it as 'complete command' and lets each compound's recorded predicates define its local use.

Senses.Explanation: In this proper-name use, Sanmei identifies a named master rather than denoting 'complete command.' Xiaotang Chaoyuan and Zhuanyu Guanheng place 'Master Sanmei' (三昧和尚) in portrait headings and call him 'a model for people and gods' (人天模範); Zhangxue Tongzui's biography of Xiaoxi records Xiaoxi receiving full ordination from him (從三昧和尚受具). These predicates belong to a person: this sense is therefore separate from compounds such as 'complete command of the single conduct' (一行三昧). The surviving witnesses also place this named master in the precept and ordination family, not in a definition of the phonetic word.
Senses.Note: Split under #0f.8 as word versus person/title. The exact form 'Master Sanmei' occurs in multiple independent allowlisted records. MasterName and SenseKey remain null because no exact canonical roster identity was established; the proper-name sense is corpus-wide lexicographic structure, not a claim of master-specific meaning.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Recorded Sayings of Master Xiaotang (笑堂和尚語錄), portrait verse headed 'Master Sanmei': Xiaotang Chaoyuan praises the named man as a model for people and gods and refers to the monastic code and precepts. Xiaotang Chaoyuan is source-attested but not yet in the roster.
